content.prompt: Calculate the value of $\theta$ in these right-angled triangles. Round your answer to 2 d.p.

spec.description: Vertical left side, horizontal base and descending hypotenuse. Right angle at lower left and theta at lower right.
spec.mathematics: Opposite side 8 and hypotenuse 9; base derived as square root of 17 and not labelled.

answer.worked:
Opposite $=8$, hypotenuse $=9$; the base is adjacent. Use sine.
$$\begin{align*}\sin\theta&=\frac{O}{H}\\\sin\theta&=\frac89\\\theta&=\sin^{-1}\left(\frac89\right)\\\theta&\approx62.73^{\circ}\end{align*}$$

answer.worked:
Opposite $=15$, adjacent $=26$; the bottom side is the hypotenuse. Use tangent.
$$\begin{align*}\tan\theta&=\frac{O}{A}\\\tan\theta&=\frac{15}{26}\\\theta&=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{15}{26}\right)\\\theta&\approx29.98^{\circ}\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: Add your answers to parts a and b. What do you notice?

answer.worked:
$$53.1^{\circ}+36.9^{\circ}=90.0^{\circ}$$
The two acute angles of a right-angled triangle add to $90^{\circ}$, since the angles of a triangle add to $180^{\circ}$ and one angle is $90^{\circ}$. So $\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{4}{3}\right)+\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)=90^{\circ}$.

children.label: d
children.prompt: Given that $\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{5}{12}\right)\approx22.6^{\circ}$, write down $\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{12}{5}\right)$ without using a calculator. Answer to 1 d.p.

answer.worked:
The ratios $\frac{5}{12}$ and $\frac{12}{5}$ give the two acute angles of the same right-angled triangle.
$$\begin{align*}\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{12}{5}\right)&=90^{\circ}-\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{5}{12}\right)\\&\approx90^{\circ}-22.6^{\circ}\\&=67.4^{\circ}\end{align*}$$

classification.difficultyReason: Parts a and b are direct applications of inverse tangent. The opposite and adjacent sides are read off a labelled right triangle, and the two parts differ only in which angle is used. Part c is guided: adding the two answers shows they make 90°. Part d is the hardest essential demand. The student must see that 5/12 and 12/5 are the two acute angles of one right triangle, and then use the complement from part c instead of calculating. This is a single reframing, and part c signposts it. It is more demanding than p35-q8, which needs only one trig choice in a half-triangle. It is less demanding than p36-q10, which needs two separate angle calculations and a comparison with a judgement about 'half'.

content.prompt:
A road rises at a grade of 3 in 10.
Find the angle (to the nearest degree) the road makes with the horizontal.

spec.description: Road slopes down from upper left to lower right above a horizontal baseline. The vertical left side is labelled 3 and the horizontal base 10. No angle label or right-angle marker is supplied.
spec.mathematics: The requested angle is at the lower-right vertex; opposite-to-adjacent ratio is 3/10.
spec.answerVisibility: Only source givens are visible; the angle value is withheld.

answer.worked:
Let $\theta$ be the angle the road makes with the horizontal. The opposite side is 3 and the adjacent side is 10.
$$\begin{align*}\tan\theta &= \frac{O}{A}\\\tan\theta &= \frac{3}{10}\\\theta &= \tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{3}{10}\right)\\\theta &\approx 17^{\circ}\quad\text{(nearest degree)}\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: Calculate the value of $\theta$ in this diagram. Answer to 1 d.p.

answer.worked:
The two horizontal lines are parallel, so $\theta$ equals the angle at the bottom of the sloping line (alternate angles). In the right-angled triangle, opposite $=6$ and hypotenuse $=10$. Use sine.
$$\begin{align*}\sin\theta&=\frac{O}{H}\\\sin\theta&=\frac{6}{10}\\\theta&=\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{6}{10}\right)\\\theta&\approx36.9^{\circ}\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: Calculate the value of $\theta$ in this diagram. Answer to 1 d.p.

answer.worked:
Let $\alpha=\angle DAB$. In the right-angled triangle with the dashed line, opposite $=5$ and hypotenuse $=7$.
$$\begin{align*}\sin\alpha&=\frac{O}{H}\\\sin\alpha&=\frac{5}{7}\\\alpha&=\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{5}{7}\right)\end{align*}$$
$AB\parallel DC$, so the interior angles on the same side of $AD$ sum to $180^{\circ}$.
$$\begin{align*}\theta&=180^{\circ}-\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{5}{7}\right)\\\theta&\approx134.4^{\circ}\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: Calculate the value of $\theta$ in this diagram. Answer to 1 d.p.

answer.worked:
Let $\alpha$ be the interior angle at the top vertex. Opposite $=8$, hypotenuse $=13$. Use sine.
$$\begin{align*}\sin\alpha&=\frac{O}{H}\\\sin\alpha&=\frac{8}{13}\\\alpha&=\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{8}{13}\right)\\\theta&=180^{\circ}-\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{8}{13}\right)\\\theta&\approx142.0^{\circ}\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: In rectangle $ABCD$, $BE$ is perpendicular to $AC$. Find the size of $\angle EBD$ to 1 d.p.

answer.worked:
In $\triangle ABC$, $\tan\angle BAC=\frac{6}{8}$, so $\angle BAC\approx36.87^\circ$. In $\triangle ABE$, $\angle AEB=90^\circ$, so $\angle ABE$ is complementary to $\angle BAC$. In $\triangle ABD$, $\tan\angle ABD=\frac{6}{8}$.
$$\begin{align*}\angle ABE&=90^\circ-36.87^\circ\\\angle ABE&=53.13^\circ\\\angle ABD&=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac68\right)\\\angle ABD&\approx36.87^\circ\\\angle EBD&=\angle ABE-\angle ABD\\\angle EBD&=53.13^\circ-36.87^\circ\\\angle EBD&\approx16.3^\circ\end{align*}$$

classification.difficultyReason: No cue is given. The student must see that the diagonals bisect each other, or use ∠ABE-∠ABD, and then combine two or three trig steps. There is no scaffolding, and the angle needs a hidden construction or difference of angles.

answer.worked:

content.prompt: $M$ is the midpoint of $AB$. Determine whether the angle $\angle ACM$ is exactly half of angle $ACB$. Give calculated angles to 1 d.p.

spec.description: Triangle CAB with horizontal CA, vertical AB, midpoint M, segments CB and CM, a midpoint dot and a right-angle square at A. Ordinary source blue strokes are rendered black under house style.
spec.mathematics: CA = 6 m; AM = MB = 2 m; CA is perpendicular to AB; M is the midpoint of AB.
spec.answerVisibility: Only source givens are visible; no calculated angles appear in the question diagram.

answer.short: No. $\angle ACM\approx18.4^\circ$ and $\angle ACB\approx33.7^\circ$, so $\angle ACM$ is not exactly half of $\angle ACB$.
answer.worked:
$AB=2+2=4\,\mathrm{m}$.

$$\begin{align*}
\tan\angle ACM&=\frac{AM}{AC}\\
\tan\angle ACM&=\frac{2}{6}\\
\angle ACM&=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{2}{6}\right)\\
\angle ACM&\approx18.4^\circ\\
\tan\angle ACB&=\frac{AB}{AC}\\
\tan\angle ACB&=\frac{4}{6}\\
\angle ACB&=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{4}{6}\right)\\
\angle ACB&\approx33.7^\circ
\end{align*}$$

Half of $\angle ACB$ is approximately $16.8^\circ$, which differs from $\angle ACM\approx18.4^\circ$. Therefore, $\angle ACM$ is not exactly half of $\angle ACB$.

content.prompt: Find the length of $BC$ to 1 d.p.

answer.worked:
Draw the perpendicular from $A$ to $BC$, meeting it at $M$. In an isosceles triangle it bisects the apex angle and the base, so $\angle BAM=48^\circ36'\div2=24^\circ18'$.
$$\begin{align*}\sin24^\circ18'&=\frac{BM}{20}\\BM&=20\sin24^\circ18'\\BM&\approx8.230\\BC&=2\times BM\\BC&\approx16.5\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$

children.prompt: Calculate the length of the ladder to the nearest cm.

spec.description: Ladder against a vertical wall; decorative brickwork and ladder rungs omitted.
spec.mathematics: The ladder is the hypotenuse; the horizontal adjacent side is 165 cm and the ground angle is 75 degrees.
spec.answerVisibility: No supplied answer appears in the question diagram.

answer.worked:
Let $L$ be the ladder length in cm.
$$\begin{align*}\cos75^\circ&=\frac{165}{L}\\L\cos75^\circ&=165\\L&=\frac{165}{\cos75^\circ}\\L&\approx638\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Calculate the horizontal distance of the person from the birds, to 1 d.p.

spec.description: Bird and person silhouettes replaced by editable role labels; both heights, dashed projections and right-angle marks retained.
spec.mathematics: The sight-line angle at the person's viewing level is 62 degrees. Birds are 2450 cm above ground and viewing level is 187 cm above ground; d is the horizontal ground distance.
spec.answerVisibility: No height difference or distance answer is supplied.

answer.worked:
The height difference is $2450-187=2263\text{ cm}$.
$$\begin{align*}\tan62^\circ&=\frac{2263}{d}\\d\tan62^\circ&=2263\\d&=\frac{2263}{\tan62^\circ}\\d&\approx1203.3\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: The slant height of the roof, to 1 d.p.

spec.description: Symmetric roof triangle with both base angles, full-span dimension, dashed altitude and external right-slope dimension; decorative chimney omitted.
spec.mathematics: Both base angles are 40 degrees, the full span is 1600 cm, and w is the right sloping side.
spec.answerVisibility: The half-span and slant-height answer are not supplied.

answer.worked:
The equal base angles make the roof triangle isosceles, so the altitude bisects the span: $1600\div2=800\text{ cm}$.
$$\begin{align*}\cos40^\circ&=\frac{800}{w}\\w\cos40^\circ&=800\\w&=\frac{800}{\cos40^\circ}\\w&\approx1044.3\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$

children.label: e
children.prompt: The angle of the leaning water tower, to the nearest minute.

spec.description: Unshaded leaning tower outline with ground, dashed vertical projection, right-angle mark and horizontal offset. The source's unattached 90 m label remains between the projection and leaning side.
spec.mathematics: The horizontal offset is 3 m; theta is the acute angle between the leaning side and leftward horizontal ground. The segment measured by 90 m is unresolved.
spec.answerVisibility: No angle answer is supplied.

answer.worked:
If $90\text{ m}$ is the vertical height:
$$\begin{align*}\tan\theta&=\frac{90}{3}\\\theta&=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{90}{3}\right)\\\theta&\approx88^\circ5'\end{align*}$$
If $90\text{ m}$ is the leaning length:
$$\begin{align*}\cos\theta&=\frac{3}{90}\\\theta&=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{3}{90}\right)\\\theta&\approx88^\circ5'\end{align*}$$
Both interpretations give the supplied answer to the nearest minute.

content.prompt:
Toby constructed two isosceles right triangles.
He says that when the two short sides are the same the angle $\theta$ is always $45^\circ$.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Show he is correct, using trigonometry in the two triangles.

spec.description: Equal perpendicular legs, Roman numeral I, and the acute theta at the bottom right.
spec.mathematics: Both legs are 12 cm; bottom-left angle is right.
spec.answerVisibility: The unknown angle is not evaluated.

spec.description: Second equal-leg triangle, positioned to the right of I for comparison.
spec.mathematics: Both legs are 17 cm; bottom-left angle is right.
spec.answerVisibility: The unknown angle is not evaluated.

answer.worked:
Triangle I:
$$\begin{align*}\tan\theta&=\frac{12}{12}\\\theta&=\tan^{-1}(1)\\\theta&=45^\circ\end{align*}$$
Triangle II:
$$\begin{align*}\tan\theta&=\frac{17}{17}\\\theta&=\tan^{-1}(1)\\\theta&=45^\circ\end{align*}$$
Both triangles have $\theta=45^\circ$, so Toby is correct.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Show he is correct, using properties of isosceles triangles and angle sum of a triangle.

answer.short: The two acute angles are equal. $2\theta+90^\circ=180^\circ$, so $\theta=45^\circ$.
answer.worked:
The angles opposite the equal sides are equal, so both acute angles are $\theta$.
$$\begin{align*}\theta+\theta+90^\circ&=180^\circ\\2\theta&=90^\circ\\\theta&=45^\circ\end{align*}$$

A roof truss is in the shape of an isosceles triangle. Each sloping beam is 4.2 m long and the base is 6 m long.
Calculate the angle $\theta$ that a beam makes with the base. Answer to the nearest minute.

answer.worked:
The triangle is isosceles, so the perpendicular from the apex bisects the base. This gives a right-angled triangle with hypotenuse $4.2$ and adjacent side $3$.
$$\begin{align*}\cos\theta&=\frac{A}{H}\\\cos\theta&=\frac{3}{4.2}\\\theta&=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{3}{4.2}\right)\\\theta&\approx44^\circ25'\end{align*}$$

The entrance to the school is 60 cm above ground level.
A wheelchair ramp is to be built at an angle of $4^{\circ}$ to the ground.
How far horizontally from the school entrance must the ramp start? Answer to the nearest cm.

answer.worked:
Let $x$ be the horizontal distance from the school entrance.

children.label: d
children.prompt:
An aircraft is at an altitude of 770 m. It is 1.5 km horizontally from the airport.
What angle must it descend by to land safely? Answer to the nearest minute.

answer.worked:
The horizontal distance is $1.5\text{ km}=1500\text{ m}$. Let $\theta$ be the angle of descent to the horizontal.
$$\begin{align*}\tan\theta&=\frac{770}{1500}\\\theta&=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{770}{1500}\right)\\\theta&\approx27.171\ldots^{\circ}\end{align*}$$
The minutes are $60\left[\tan^{-1}(770/1500)-27^{\circ}\right]\approx10.27'$, so $\theta\approx27^{\circ}10'$.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\cos 51^{\circ}38' &= \frac{AB}{9.4}\\AB &= 9.4\cos 51^{\circ}38'\\\sin 51^{\circ}38' &= \frac{BC}{9.4}\\BC &= 9.4\sin 51^{\circ}38'\end{align*}$$

$$\begin{align*}AB+BC &= 9.4\cos 51^{\circ}38'+9.4\sin 51^{\circ}38'\\&\approx 13.2\ \mathrm{m}\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: A rectangular paddock $ABCD$ has a diagonal track $AC$ of length 640 m that makes an angle of $37^{\circ}20'$ with side $AB$. Fencing is needed along $AB$ and $BC$. Find the total length of fencing, in metres correct to the nearest metre.

answer.worked:
The paddock is a rectangle, so triangle $ABC$ is right-angled at $B$ with hypotenuse $AC=640$.
$$\begin{align*}\cos37^{\circ}20'&=\frac{AB}{640}\\AB&=640\cos37^{\circ}20'\\\sin37^{\circ}20'&=\frac{BC}{640}\\BC&=640\sin37^{\circ}20'\end{align*}$$
The total length of fencing is the sum of the two sides.
$$\begin{align*}AB+BC&=640\cos37^{\circ}20'+640\sin37^{\circ}20'\\&\approx897\text{ m}\end{align*}$$

children.prompt: Show that $AC=7\tan50^{\circ}$ and $BC=7\tan25^{\circ}$, and hence find the length $AB$, correct to 1 mm.

spec.description: Two right triangles share DC. A, B and C lie on the same vertical line; the two adjacent angles at D are each 25 degrees.
spec.mathematics: DC=7 cm; angle BDC=25 degrees; angle ADB=25 degrees; angle DCA=90 degrees; B lies between A and C.
spec.answerVisibility: Only source givens are visible.

answer.worked:
In $\triangle ADC$, $\angle ADC=25^{\circ}+25^{\circ}=50^{\circ}$.
$$\begin{align*}\tan50^{\circ}&=\frac{AC}{7}\\AC&=7\tan50^{\circ}\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$
In $\triangle BDC$:
$$\begin{align*}\tan25^{\circ}&=\frac{BC}{7}\\BC&=7\tan25^{\circ}\text{ cm}\\AB&=AC-BC\\AB&=7(\tan50^{\circ}-\tan25^{\circ})\text{ cm}\\AB&=70(\tan50^{\circ}-\tan25^{\circ})\text{ mm}\\AB&\approx51\text{ mm}\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Show that $AP=20\sin56^{\circ}$, and hence find the length of $PC$, giving your answer correct to 1 cm.

spec.description: Triangle ABC is divided by perpendicular AP, with P between B and C.
spec.mathematics: AB=20 cm; angle ABC=56 degrees; angle ACB=46 degrees; AP is perpendicular to BC.
spec.answerVisibility: Only source givens are visible.

answer.worked:
In $\triangle ABP$:
$$\begin{align*}\sin56^{\circ}&=\frac{AP}{20}\\AP&=20\sin56^{\circ}\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$
In $\triangle APC$:
$$\begin{align*}\tan46^{\circ}&=\frac{AP}{PC}\\PC\tan46^{\circ}&=AP\\PC&=\frac{20\sin56^{\circ}}{\tan46^{\circ}}\\PC&\approx16\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: Show that $PR=18\cos40^{\circ}$, find an expression for $PQ$, and hence find the angle $\alpha$, correct to the nearest minute.

spec.description: Right triangle PQR contains QS. S lies between P and R; alpha marks the acute interior angle PSQ.
spec.mathematics: QR=18 cm; SR=8 cm; angle PRQ=40 degrees; angle QPR=90 degrees; alpha=angle PSQ.
spec.answerVisibility: Only source givens are visible.

answer.worked:
In $\triangle PQR$:
$$\begin{align*}\cos40^{\circ}&=\frac{PR}{18}\\PR&=18\cos40^{\circ}\text{ cm}\\\sin40^{\circ}&=\frac{PQ}{18}\\PQ&=18\sin40^{\circ}\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$
Since $SR=8$ cm:
$$\begin{align*}PS&=PR-SR\\PS&=18\cos40^{\circ}-8\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$
In $\triangle PSQ$:
$$\begin{align*}\tan\alpha&=\frac{PQ}{PS}\\\tan\alpha&=\frac{18\sin40^{\circ}}{18\cos40^{\circ}-8}\\\alpha&=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{18\sin40^{\circ}}{18\cos40^{\circ}-8}\right)\\\alpha&\approx63^{\circ}25'\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: A bridge spans a river, and the two identical sections of the bridge, each of length $x$ metres, can be raised to allow tall boats to pass. When the two sections are fully raised, they are each inclined at $50^\circ$ to the horizontal, and there is an 18-metre gap between them, as shown in the diagram. Calculate the width of the river in metres, correct to one decimal place.

spec.description: Symmetric raised bridge sections, dashed horizontal gap and baseline, and circular swing arcs terminating at the common closed-position midpoint. Ordinary source marks are rendered black without shading.
spec.mathematics: Each bridge section has length x. Each rises at 50 degrees to the horizontal. The horizontal distance between raised endpoints is 18 m. The closed sections meet at the baseline midpoint, so the river width is 2x. Drawing coordinates express these relationships without introducing additional numerical givens.
spec.answerVisibility: Only source givens are visible; no calculated width or section length is shown.

answer.worked:
The closed sections meet at the midpoint, so the river is $2x$ metres wide. Each raised section has horizontal projection $x\cos50^\circ$.
$$\begin{align*}
2x-2x\cos50^\circ &= 18\\
2x(1-\cos50^\circ) &= 18\\
2x &= \frac{18}{1-\cos50^\circ}\\
2x &\approx 50.4\,\mathrm{m}
\end{align*}$$
The river is $50.4\,\mathrm{m}$ wide, correct to one decimal place.

Find $AC$ in $\Delta ABC$ and $DC$ in $\Delta BDC$ using $\tan$, then subtract: $AD = AC - DC$.
answer.worked:
Find the full base $AC$ in the large right-angled triangle $ABC$, then subtract $DC$ from the smaller right-angled triangle $BDC$.
In $\Delta ABC$:
$$\begin{align*}\tan(25^\circ) &= \frac{100}{AC}\\AC &= \frac{100}{\tan(25^\circ)}\\&\approx 214.450\text{ m}\end{align*}$$
In $\Delta BDC$:
$$\begin{align*}\tan(76^\circ) &= \frac{100}{DC}\\DC &= \frac{100}{\tan(76^\circ)}\\&\approx 24.932\text{ m}\end{align*}$$
Therefore:
$$\begin{align*}AD &= AC - DC\\&= 214.450 - 24.932\\&\approx 190\text{ m}\end{align*}$$
Answer: (C).

content.prompt:
An observer is on top of a building at $A$.
A second, taller, building is $12$ metres away on level ground.
From $A$, the angle of elevation to the top of the other building is $35^\circ$ and the angle of depression to the base is $50^\circ$.
Find the height, to 1 decimal place, of the taller building.

answer.worked:
The vertical distance from $A$ down to the base is:
$$\begin{align*}
h_1 &= 12\tan 50^\circ \\
&\approx 14.301
\end{align*}$$
The vertical distance from $A$ up to the top is:
$$\begin{align*}
h_2 &= 12\tan 35^\circ \\
&\approx 8.402
\end{align*}$$
The total height is:
$$\begin{align*}
h &= h_1 + h_2 \\
&\approx 14.301 + 8.402 \\
&\approx 22.703
\end{align*}$$
The height of the taller building is $22.7\text{ m}$.

content.prompt: Calculate the area of this trapezium.

answer.short: $81\text{ cm}^2$. Use the $36^\circ52'$ angle in a right-angled triangle to find $h$, then the trapezium area formula.
answer.worked:
The horizontal difference between the parallel sides is $21-15=6\text{ cm}$.
The acute angle at the top right is $180^\circ - 143^\circ8' = 36^\circ52'$.
$$\begin{align*}
\tan(36^\circ52') &= \frac{h}{6} \\
h &= 6\tan(36^\circ52') \\
&\approx 4.4994\text{ cm}
\end{align*}$$
Now find the area of the trapezium.
$$\begin{align*}
A &= \frac{1}{2}(15+21)h \\
&= 18(4.4994\ldots) \\
&= 80.989\ldots
\end{align*}$$
The area is approximately $81\text{ cm}^2$.

content.prompt:
A point $P$ lies between a tree, $2\text{ metres}$ high, and a tower, $8\text{ metres}$ high.

$P$ is $3\text{ metres}$ away from the base of the tree.

From $P$, the angles of elevation to the top of the tree and to the top of the tower are equal.

What is the distance, $x$, from $P$ to the top of the tower?

A. $9\text{ m}$

B. $9.61\text{ m}$

C. $12.04\text{ m}$

D. $14.42\text{ m}$

spec.description: A 2 m tree and an 8 m tower stand on opposite sides of P. The tree base is 3 m from P. The two elevation angles are marked equal, both bases are marked perpendicular, and x labels the sightline to the tower top. The figure is marked not to scale.

answer.worked:
Let $\theta$ be the common angle of elevation and $y$ the horizontal distance from $P$ to the tower base in metres. The two right triangles give

$$\tan\theta=\frac23=\frac8y,$$

so $y=12$. By Pythagoras,

$$x=\sqrt{8^2+12^2}\text{ m}=\sqrt{208}\text{ m}\approx14.42\text{ m}.$$

The correct choice is D.

classification.difficultyReason: Mastery: two linked right-triangle calculations must be combined as a distance difference, then converted to speed in different units.

content.prompt:
A plane is flying at a height of $900$ metres above ground. From a point $P$ on the ground, the angle of elevation to the plane was $68.5^\circ$ and $20$ seconds later the angle of elevation from $P$ had changed to $25.2^\circ$.

How far had the plane flown in that time and what was its speed to the nearest $\mathrm{km/h}$?

spec.description: Two sightlines rise to the right from P to successive positions at the same height of 900 m. The nearer sightline makes 68.5° with the ground and the farther sightline makes 25.2°. A horizontal arrow points from the first position to the second.

answer.worked:
Let $x_1$ and $x_2$ be the horizontal distances from $P$ to the first and second plane positions.

$$x_1=\frac{900}{\tan 68.5^\circ}\approx354.52\,\mathrm{m},\qquad x_2=\frac{900}{\tan25.2^\circ}\approx1912.60\,\mathrm{m}.$$

The plane travels $d=x_2-x_1\approx1558.08\,\mathrm{m}$. The elapsed time is $20/3600=1/180$ hours. Using the unrounded distance,

$$v=\frac{180}{1000}\left(\frac{900}{\tan25.2^\circ}-\frac{900}{\tan68.5^\circ}\right)\approx280.45\,\mathrm{km/h},$$

which rounds to $280\,\mathrm{km/h}$.

classification.difficultyReason: Mastery: the student must infer equal overhangs, express the height symbolically using tangent, and combine it with the trapezium area formula.

content.prompt:
Find an expression for the area of the trapezium below.

A. $\frac{1}{4}(q^2-p^2)\tan\theta$

B. $\frac{1}{4}(q^2-p^2)\cot\theta$

C. $\frac{1}{2}(q^2-p^2)\tan\theta$

D. $\frac{1}{2}(q^2+p^2)\tan\theta$

spec.description: Trapezium with upper parallel side p, lower parallel side q and both lower interior angles marked θ.

answer.worked:
The equal base angles give a horizontal overhang of $\frac{q-p}{2}$ on each side. Using tangent, the height is $h=\frac{q-p}{2}\tan\theta$.

$$\begin{aligned}A&=\tfrac12(p+q)h\\&=\tfrac14(p+q)(q-p)\tan\theta\\&=\tfrac14(q^2-p^2)\tan\theta.\end{aligned}$$

The correct choice is A.

content.prompt:
Eflal is approximately $170\text{ cm}$ tall.

To calculate the height of a building, she stands at a point and measures the angle of elevation to the top of the building as $45^\circ$.

She then walks $25.7$ metres further away from the building and measures the angle of elevation as $30^\circ$.

Find the height of the building, correct to the nearest metre.

Draw a diagram to support your response.

answer.worked:
Let $h$ be the building height in metres and $d$ the horizontal distance from the closer observation point to the building, in metres. Using $1.7\text{ m}$ as Eflal's eye height gives a rise of $h-1.7$ metres to the top of the building.

$$\tan45^\circ=\frac{h-1.7}{d}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad d=h-1.7.$$

The farther observation point is $d+25.7=h+24$ metres from the building.

$$\begin{aligned}\tan30^\circ&=\frac{h-1.7}{h+24}\\ h+24&=\sqrt3(h-1.7)\\ h(\sqrt3-1)&=24+1.7\sqrt3\\ h&\approx36.8069.\end{aligned}$$

The building is $37\text{ m}$ high to the nearest metre.

spec.description: Two observation points A and C at the same eye level, 25.7 m apart, with 30° and 45° sightlines to B. D is level with the observation points and directly below B. Vertical dimensions show the eye height, the rise above eye level and the full building height.

classification.difficultyReason: Challenge: the student must introduce a useful perpendicular, solve two linked right triangles, and subtract angles.

content.prompt:
What is the value of $\theta$, to the nearest degree?

A. $21^\circ$

B. $32^\circ$

C. $43^\circ$

D. $55^\circ$

spec.description: Nested right triangles share the left vertical leg. The inner hypotenuse is 100 m and θ lies between it and the vertical. The external horizontal segment between the upper inner vertex and outer right vertex is 82 m. The angle at the outer right vertex is 26°. The figure is marked not to scale.

answer.worked:
Let $\phi$ be the angle between the two sloping sides at the bottom vertex. Drop a perpendicular from the upper end of the $100\text{ m}$ side to the long sloping side. In the right triangle at the outer right vertex, the perpendicular is opposite $26^\circ$ and the hypotenuse is $82\text{ m}$, so the perpendicular has length $82\sin26^\circ$ metres.

In the other right triangle formed by the perpendicular, the hypotenuse is $100\text{ m}$ and the perpendicular is opposite $\phi$.

$$\sin\phi=\frac{82\sin26^\circ}{100}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\phi\approx21.07^\circ.$$

The bottom angle of the outer triangle is $90^\circ-26^\circ=64^\circ$. Therefore $\theta=64^\circ-\phi\approx42.93^\circ$, which rounds to $43^\circ$. The correct choice is C.

sourceCorrection.basis: The supplied solution treats the exterior 82 m horizontal segment as the side opposite θ in the triangle with hypotenuse 100 m. Image 1 and the required source review place the 82 m segment between the two upper endpoints of the sloping sides.
sourceCorrection.printedChanges: The short answer changes from D, 55°, to C, 43°. The worked solution uses the perpendicular from the inner upper vertex to the long sloping side to obtain φ = arcsin(82 sin 26° / 100), then subtracts φ from 64°. The question diagram and all four choices retain their source givens.

content.prompt: Consider the diagram.

spec.description: Unshaded triangle QPS, right-angled at P, with perpendicular altitude PR to the horizontal baseline QS. All ordinary outlines and labels use black. Coordinates are schematic and enforce both right angles without asserting numerical measurements.
spec.mathematics: Q, R and S are collinear in that order; PR is perpendicular to QS; PQ is perpendicular to PS; QR=a, RS=b, PR=h and angle PQS=theta.
spec.answerVisibility: All vertex names, side labels, theta and both right-angle markers are permanent student-visible givens.

answer.worked:
In right-angled triangle $QPR$, $\angle QPR=90^\circ-\theta$. Since $\angle QPS=90^\circ$,
$$\begin{align*}\angle RPS&=90^\circ-(90^\circ-\theta)\\&=\theta.\end{align*}$$

Using opposite over adjacent in triangles $QPR$ and $PRS$, respectively:
$$\begin{align*}\tan\theta&=\frac{h}{a}\\\tan\theta&=\frac{b}{h}.\end{align*}$$

Equate the two expressions for $\tan\theta$ and multiply both sides by $ah$:
$$\begin{align*}\frac{h}{a}&=\frac{b}{h}\\h^2&=ab\\ab&=h^2.\end{align*}$$

Finding: The first isosceles-triangle trigonometry task requires students to introduce an auxiliary altitude before any preceding instruction shows that construction.
Breakdown: The supplied triangle is not right-angled. Students must construct a right triangle and recognise its adjacent side as half the labelled base before applying the taught method. Earlier examples supply their right triangles.

Assumes: Basic isosceles properties are prior knowledge; applying an auxiliary altitude to start a trigonometric solution has not been established.

Finding: The sexagesimal topic combines earlier side and angle methods without an opening review of ratio selection, the two side-equation arrangements and inverse trigonometry.

Checked: The methods are taught in p21, p25–p26 and p31. The p40 and p41 examples use them directly. There is no review in the sexagesimal topic. (d) Solve tan theta = 5/8, giving the acute angle in decimal degrees to 2 d.p. Answer: theta = 32.01°. Keep the review within one page. Show the triangle diagrams, do not describe the triangles and do not have redundant instruction text that describes the triangle..

[Pedagogy audit v2 · New teaching] The Problem-Solving lesson never shows splitting a figure into two right triangles and adding or subtracting the segment lengths. Add a worked example of this before the exercise, since questions 12, 14, 15 and 16 depend on it.
Worked example: Find the length $AB$ in this triangle. Answer to 2 d.p.
Draw the perpendicular from $T$ to $AB$, meeting it at $F$. This splits the triangle into two right-angled triangles, $ATF$ and $TFB$, that share the side $TF$.
$$\begin{align*}TF&=9\sin50^{\circ}\\AF&=9\cos50^{\circ}\\\tan35^{\circ}&=\frac{TF}{FB}\\FB&=\frac{9\sin50^{\circ}}{\tan35^{\circ}}\\AB&=AF+FB\\AB&=9\cos50^{\circ}+\frac{9\sin50^{\circ}}{\tan35^{\circ}}\\AB&\approx15.63\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$
Guided practice:

b) (with a diagram)
c) (with a diagram)
Answers: a) $19.44\text{ cm}$; b) $22.62\text{ m}$; c) $12.76\text{ cm}$

entries.description:
Syllabus Content
MA5-TRG-C-01 applies trigonometric ratios to solve right-angled triangle problems

Demonstrate and explain the constancy of trigonometric ratios for a given angle in a right-angled triangle
• Identify and label the hypotenuse, adjacent and opposite sides with respect to a given angle in a right-angled triangle in any orientation
• Define the sine, cosine and tangent ratios for angles in right-angled triangles and use trigonometric notation sin θ, cos θ, tan θ
• Identify the sine, cosine and tangent ratios in a right-angled triangle
• Verify the constancy of the sine, cosine and tangent ratios for a given angle by applying knowledge of similar right-angled triangles
• Find approximations of the trigonometric ratios for a given angle
• Find the size of an angle given one of the trigonometric ratios for the angle using digital tools

Apply trigonometry to solve right-angled triangle problems
• Apply trigonometry to find the lengths of unknown sides in right-angled triangles with a given angle including angles in degrees and minutes
• Apply trigonometry to find the size of unknown angles in right-angled triangles including in degrees and minutes
• Solve a variety of practical problems involving trigonometric ratios in right-angled triangles
